candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 47:1 (Moses' birth (47:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And in the seventh week, in the seventh year, in the forty-seventh jubilee, thy father went forth from the land of Canaan, and thou wast born in the fourth week, in the sixth year thereof, in the forty-eighth jubilee; this was the time of tribulation on the children of Israel' — Jubilees precisely dates Moses' birth to a canonical-tribulation-period (parallel to the canonical-precision of Christ's birth being dated to a tribulation-period under Herod). Tewahedo Mosaic-Christological typology reads this as the doubled OT-NT pattern: the deliverer is born in the canonical-tribulation-context; the Herod-figure (whether Pharaoh of Ex 1 or Herod of Mt 2) seeks the deliverer's life from his infancy. The Tewahedo Holy Innocents commemoration draws on this canonical-doubled deliverer-imperilled-from-birth pattern.

candidates.draft_body:

'And there was great oppression of the children of Israel in Egypt, and they cried unto the Lord their God, and He heard their voice, and remembered His covenant with their fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and He sent His angels and led them out from Egypt' — the compressed Exodus motif: God hears the cry, remembers the covenant, sends His angels. Tewahedo exodus-theology preserves the angelic-mediation element prominently (alongside Moses' human agency), drawing on Jubilees as scriptural anchor for the angelic-historical-action doctrine.

candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 47:5 (Moses' birth (47:5)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And thy mother hid thee three months, and they told regarding her. And she made an ark for thee, and covered it with pitch and asphalt, and placed it in the flags on the bank of the river, and she placed thee in it three days, and thy sister Miriam guarded thee from a distance' — Jubilees preserves the Ex 2:1-4 Moses-in-the-ark narrative with the explicit three-day-detail. The Tewahedo Moses-as-Christ-type tradition reads the three-day-ark-in-the-water as the canonical OT prefiguration of Christ's three-day burial. The 'placed three days' detail (which is not in Exodus) anchors the typological reading: Moses-in-the-ark for three days = Christ-in-the-tomb for three days. Tewahedo Easter-vigil liturgy preserves the Moses-ark / Christ-tomb correspondence in the readings.

candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 47:9 (Moses' birth (47:9)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And the daughter of Pharaoh came to bathe in the river, and she heard thy voice crying, and she told her maidens to bring thee forth, and they brought thee unto her. And she took thee out of the ark, and she had compassion on thee. And thy sister said unto her: shall I go and call to thee one of the Hebrew women, who shall nurse and suckle this babe for thee? And she said unto her: go. And she went and called thy mother, and she gave her wages, and she nursed thee' — Moses is rescued by the daughter of Pharaoh, suckled by his own mother. Tewahedo readings preserve a canonical-irony: the daughter of the persecutor is the deliverer's first-Gentile-protector. The Tewahedo distinctive pastoral practice of warmly welcoming and catechizing the children of those who persecuted the Tewahedo (the children of fascist-occupation-collaborators after 1941, for example) draws canonical anchor from Pharaoh's-daughter's-compassion canonical category.

'And thy mother hid thee three months, and they told regarding her. And she made an ark for thee, and covered it with pitch and asphalt, and placed it in the flags on the bank of the river, and she placed thee in it three days, and thy sister Miriam guarded thee from a distance' — Jubilees preserves the Ex 2:1-4 Moses-in-the-ark narrative with the explicit three-day-detail. The Tewahedo Moses-as-Christ-type tradition reads the three-day-ark-in-the-water as the canonical OT prefiguration of Christ's three-day burial. The 'placed three days' detail (which is not in Exodus) anchors the typological reading: Moses-in-the-ark for three days = Christ-in-the-tomb for three days. Tewahedo Easter-vigil liturgy preserves the Moses-ark / Christ-tomb correspondence in the readings.

Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And the daughter of Pharaoh came to bathe in the river, and she heard thy voice crying, and she told her maidens to bring thee forth, and they brought thee unto her. And she took thee out of the ark, and she had compassion on thee. And thy sister said unto her: shall I go and call to thee one of the Hebrew women, who shall nurse and suckle this babe for thee? And she said unto her: go. And she went and called thy mother, and she gave her wages, and she nursed thee' — Moses is rescued by the daughter of Pharaoh, suckled by his own mother. Tewahedo readings preserve a canonical-irony: the daughter of the persecutor is the deliverer's first-Gentile-protector. The Tewahedo distinctive pastoral practice of warmly welcoming and catechizing the children of those who persecuted the Tewahedo (the children of fascist-occupation-collaborators after 1941, for example) draws canonical anchor from Pharaoh's-daughter's-compassion canonical category.
